Lessons.Title: What’s the Equation?
ExplanationParagraphs: Use sequences to model contexts, state valid discrete domains, and compare recursive and explicit representations.

A model needs a meaningful domain as well as a rule. For a 4-by-4 subdivision where each new piece has a quarter of the previous area, an 80-square-inch region creates A(1)=80, A(n)=80*(1/4)^(n-1); the first four areas are 80,20,5,1.25. In a line of n joined hexagonal tables, one table exposes 6 sides and each additional table adds 4 usable sides, so P(n)=6+4(n-1)=4n+2 for positive integer n. A paper or table count cannot sensibly be evaluated at a fractional n.

First-party independent cool-down: An envelope starts at 6.75 grams and each inserted clip adds 0.5 grams. Define w(n) for n nonnegative clips, find w(5), and explain why w(2.5) is not an appropriate count of clips. Answer key: w(n)=6.75+0.5n; w(5)=9.25 grams; n is a nonnegative integer.

KeyConcepts.Title: Domain from context
KeyConcepts.Rule: Tables and people require whole nonnegative or positive numbers.

KeyConcepts.Title: Linear pattern
KeyConcepts.Definition: An equal increase each step yields an arithmetic sequence.
KeyConcepts.Example: Three connected hexagonal tables seat 14 people.

KeyConcepts.Title: Quarter-area decay
KeyConcepts.Definition: Repeated division by 4 produces geometric decrease.

WorkedExamples.Title: Connected tables
WorkedExamples.Question: How many places around five joined hexagonal tables?
WorkedExamples.Method: Start with 6 and add 4 per additional table.
WorkedExamples.Check: Each joined edge removes one exposed side from each of two tables.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating a sequence rule as context-free.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: It can alter the index, initial term, units or learning target.
CommonMistakes.Correction: State the beginning term, domain and original lesson model.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using a fixed common difference when the sequence is not arithmetic.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Differing consecutive differences invalidate the arithmetic formula.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Calculate two or more differences or ratios before selecting a rule.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Auto-grading graphs, card exchanges or manipulative proof from a number alone.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Numeric equality does not establish a correct diagram or explanation.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use a teacher rubric for visual and reasoning evidence.
